'''Herbert Kroemer''' ({{IPA|de|ˈhɛʁbɛʁt ˈkʁøːmɐ|lang|De-Herbert Kroemer.ogg}}; August 25, 1928 – March 8, 2024) was a German–American theoretical [[physicist]] who shared one half of the 2000 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Zhores Alferov]] "for developing semiconductor [[heterostructure]]s used in high-speed- and opto-electronics."<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2000 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/summary/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081021034902/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2000/index.html|archive-date=2008-10-21|access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref> His research into [[transistor]]s was a stepping stone to the later development of [[mobile phone]] technologies.

== Biography ==
=== Education ===
Herbert Kroemer was born on August 25, 1928, in [[Weimar]], [[State of Thuringia (1920–1952)|State of Thuringia]], Germany. His father was a civil servant, while his mother was a housewife; neither of them had a high school education. After graduating from ''[[Gymnasium (school)|Gymnasium]]'' in 1947, Kroemer entered the [[University of Jena]], where he studied physics under [[Friedrich Hund]]. By early 1948, the political suppression in [[Soviet occupation zone in Germany|Soviet-occupied Germany]] became very severe; he recalls that every week, some of his fellow students had suddenly disappeared. In the summer of 1948, Kroemer worked for [[Siemens]] in Berlin. During the [[Berlin Blockade]], he was airlifted out of Berlin and moved to [[West Germany]] to continue his education.<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=Herbert Kroemer – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kroemer/biographical/|publisher=NobelPrize.org|access-date=November 5, 2026}}</ref>

Having been initially rejected, Kroemer was accepted as a student by the [[University of Göttingen]], where he was supervised by [[Fritz Sauter]] for a ''[[Diplom]]''. His ''Diplom'' thesis was an extension of [[William Shockley]]'s 1939 paper on the nature of [[surface state]]s in one-dimensional potentials.<ref name="Nobel bio"/> In 1952, he received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in Theoretical Physics for a thesis on hot-electron effects in the then-new [[transistor]].<ref name="engineering">{{Cite web |title=Nobel Laureate Herb Kroemer, 1928–2024 |url=https://engineering.ucsb.edu/news/nobel-laureate-herb-kroemer-1928-2024|publisher=UC Santa Barbara College of Engineering|date=March 12, 2024|access-date=March 13, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Kroemer|first=Herbert|year=1953|title=Zur Theorie des Germaniumgleichrichters und des Transistors : Ausz. Mit 10 Fig. im Text|url=https://d-nb.info/480389888 |degree=Ph.D.|language=de|publisher=German National Library|oclc=73916980}}</ref>

=== Career ===
Unable to find work at a university as a new graduate, Kroemer became a "house theorist" at the Central Telecommunications Laboratory of the [[Deutsche Bundespost]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/> In 1954, he immigrated to the United States, where he worked for the [[Radio Corporation of America]] (1954–1957), [[Varian Associates]] (1959–1966), and [[Fairchild Semiconductor]] (1966–1968).<ref name="AIP"/>

In 1968, Kroemer was appointed Professor of Electrical Engineering at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]].<ref name="encyclopedia">{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Herbert Kroemer |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbert-Kroemer|url-status=live |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251016202510/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbert-Kroemer|archive-date=2025-10-16|access-date=2026-06-29}}</ref> In 1976, he joined the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] (UCSB), focusing its semiconductor research program on the emerging compound semiconductor technology rather than on mainstream [[silicon]] technology.<ref name="ECE">{{Cite web |title=Professor Herbert Kroemer |url=http://www.ece.ucsb.edu/faculty/Kroemer/default.html|url-status=dead|department=Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering |publisher=UCSB|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080922213953/http://www.ece.ucsb.edu/faculty/Kroemer/default.html|archive-date=2008-09-22|access-date=2026-06-29}}</ref> He held the Donald W. Whittier Chair of Electrical Engineering at UCSB until his retirement as professor emeritus in 2012.<ref name="chancellor">{{Cite web|title=Sad News - Professor Emeritus Herbert Kroemer |url=https://chancellor.ucsb.edu/memos/2024-03-12-sad-news-professor-emeritus-herbert-kroemer |publisher=UC Santa Barbara Office of the Chancellor|date=12 March 2024|access-date=13 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="encyclopedia"/>

== Research ==
Kroemer always preferred to work on problems that are ahead of mainstream technology, being the first to point out in the mid-1950s that advantages could be gained in various semiconductor devices by incorporating [[heterojunction]]s.<ref name="ECE"/> Most notably, in 1963, he proposed the concept of the [[Quantum well laser|double-heterostructure laser]], which is now a central concept in the field of [[semiconductor laser]]s. Kroemer became an early pioneer in [[molecular-beam epitaxy]], concentrating on applying the technology to untried new materials.<ref name="engineering"/>

[[Charles Kittel]] had published the successful ''Thermal Physics'' in 1969, and enlisted Kroemer to edit it for a second edition, which appeared in 1980. Kroemer is also the author of the textbook ''Quantum Mechanics for Engineering, Materials Science and Applied Physics''.<ref>H. Kroemer, Quantum Mechanics, Prentice Hall (1994)</ref>

== Personal life ==
Kroemer was an [[atheist]].<ref>Kroemer, Herbert. "Herbert Kroemer – Science Video Interview". Interviewer: "You have no belief in a afterlife?" Kroemer: "That's correct." Interviewer: "...You don't see the evidence of a designer?" Kroemer: "No, I don't." Interviewer: "Could you say more about it?" Kroemer: "I think it's just wishful thinking."</ref> He became a [[naturalized U.S. citizen]] in 2003.<ref name="chancellor"/>

Kroemer died on March 8, 2024, in [[Santa Barbara, California]], at the age of 95.<ref name="chancellor"/><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/herbert-kroemer-nachruf-a-a595715a-0357-4080-9a44-c8f26926f654 | title=Nachruf: Herbert Kroemer | newspaper=Der Spiegel | date=15 March 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2024/03/28/herbert-kroemer-dead/ | title=Herbert Kroemer, Nobel winner who developed laser tech, dies at 95 | newspaper=The Washington Post | date=2024-03-28}}</ref>
